forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of $2.01 remains 17% above Street consensus of $1.72, reflecting what I view as systematic underestimation of mechanical EPS drivers that persist quarter after quarter. The key insight is that Wall Street is not fully pricing in the EPS accretion from (1) accelerated share buybacks at depressed prices - with ~$220M quarterly buybacks at ~$175 average, diluted shares should decline to ~170.8M versus Q3's 174.6M, contributing approximately $0.04-0.05 in per-share accretion; (2) declining interest expense to ~$82M versus $87M in Q3 as debt paydown continues at pace; and (3) SG&A normalization despite CEO transition costs of ~$10M. The AB InBev Q4 2025 results showing 6% underlying EPS growth and continued margin expansion validate the beer category's resilience.

Revenue is capped at ~$2.17B by seasonal patterns - Q4 is consistently the weakest quarter for Constellation, and I see no catalyst to break this pattern. The beer segment should deliver ~$2.0B with flat-to-slightly-negative volumes offset by 2-3% price/mix benefits. Wine & Spirits continues to decline post-divestitures at ~$170M. Gross margin should hold at ~52% reflecting stable beer mix and input cost management.

The key risks to my thesis are: (1) if consumer demand softness materializes more acutely in premium beer, which could pressure volumes beyond my -1% assumption; (2) if CEO transition costs come in higher than the ~$10M I'm modeling in SG&A; and (3) if tariff escalation impacts input costs more than currently anticipated. However, the news flow remains supportive with no negative operational signals, and the February 12 8-K confirms orderly CEO succession. I'm maintaining my above-consensus view with medium conviction given the mechanical nature of the EPS drivers.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of ¥38.50 represents a 6.9% premium to Street consensus of ¥36.03, driven primarily by the market's underappreciation of share count reduction from Seven & i's aggressive buyback program. The share count trajectory is undeniable: declining from 2.60B in Q4 FY25 to 2.44B in Q3 FY26 (a 6% reduction in three quarters). Assuming a continued buyback pace of ~¥89B quarterly (conservative vs Q3's exceptional ¥162B), I project share count declining to approximately 2.18B by Q4 FY26. This mechanical EPS lift is being underweighted by consensus, which appears to be anchoring on stale share count assumptions.

The revenue picture supports modest growth to ¥2,475B, up 1.8% QoQ driven by seasonal Q4 strength in convenience stores. Walmart and CVS Q4 results confirm a healthy US consumer environment that benefits 7-Eleven North America - the company's profit engine. The key uncertainty remains gross margin: Q3's anomalous 29.1% (vs historical 19-21%) appears related to one-time items or accounting shifts rather than sustainable improvement. I'm assuming normalization to 26.5%, which is still elevated but more defensible. Operating margin should reach 5.6% on seasonal leverage.

What would change my view: (1) If the buyback pace slows dramatically due to Couche-Tard acquisition negotiations creating capital deployment uncertainty, the EPS uplift would diminish significantly. (2) If gross margin collapses back to historical 19-20% levels, that would indicate Q3 was truly anomalous and my estimates would need to come down ¥5-8. (3) Material yen appreciation against USD would create translation headwinds on North American earnings. I maintain medium-high conviction given the mechanical nature of the share count reduction thesis, though gross margin uncertainty keeps me from higher conviction.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS forecast of ¥39.0 for Seven & i Holdings represents a slight upward revision from my previous ¥38.5 estimate, reflecting continued execution on the company's capital return strategy and stable operating fundamentals. The Wall Street consensus figure of $0.19 is clearly erroneous - this appears to be a data provider error involving currency conversion or decimal placement, as the historical EPS data shows quarterly earnings consistently in the ¥19-42 range. Using proper yen-denominated analysis, my estimate implies a modest sequential improvement from Q3's ¥33.0 driven by Q4's seasonal strength (holiday/new year period in Japan, strong December in North America).

The key drivers supporting my thesis are: (1) North American convenience store operations remain healthy, supported by Walmart's Q4 2026 results showing consumer strength across income cohorts - this is directly relevant as 7-Eleven competes for the same convenience-oriented spending; (2) The aggressive buyback program has reduced share count from 2.60B in Q4 2025 to an estimated 2.35B in Q4 2026, providing ~10% EPS accretion even on flat earnings; (3) Gross margins have stabilized around 29% following earlier normalization. My revenue estimate of ¥2.485T reflects typical Q4 seasonal strength (~1-2% above Q3) without aggressive assumptions.

What would change my view: A significant deterioration in Japan consumer sentiment, acceleration of the Couche-Tard takeover process creating operational disruption, or unexpected one-time charges from supermarket segment restructuring. The primary risk to my estimate is that Q4's operating income might not recover as strongly as I project from Q3's ¥120B if SG&A costs remain elevated. However, the continued buyback execution provides a meaningful cushion to EPS even if operating metrics slightly disappoint.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.53 remains $0.02 (3.6%) below consensus of $0.55, driven primarily by my view that Wall Street is underweighting the tax rate normalization headwind. Q4 2025's effective tax rate of 2.6% ($109M on $4.26B pretax income) was anomalously low due to discrete tax benefits and will revert to AT&T's normalized 21% range in Q1. This single factor creates approximately $900M in net income headwind versus Q4, which I believe consensus has not fully incorporated. The street appears to be extrapolating Q4's strong beat without adequately adjusting for the non-recurring nature of the tax benefit.

From a revenue perspective, I expect Q1 to come in around $30.75B, roughly flat sequentially but reflecting a significant mix shift. Equipment revenue will decline approximately 16% QoQ from Q4's holiday-elevated levels, while wireless service revenue continues its steady 2-3% YoY growth trajectory. The fiber business remains a bright spot with ~260K quarterly net adds and ARPU expansion, but this positive momentum is offset by ongoing legacy wireline erosion. The Cisco partnership for 5G Standalone IoT is strategically interesting but won't materially impact 2026 financials.

What would change my view: (1) If tax rate guidance in the upcoming CFO conference appearance suggests a lower-than-expected normalized rate, I would revise upward; (2) If wireless promotional activity proves less intense than Bernstein's warnings suggest, ARPU could surprise positively; (3) Faster-than-expected fiber subscriber acceleration could add $0.01-0.02 to my estimate. The key swing factor remains the tax rate - if AT&T has additional discrete benefits available in Q1, consensus could prove correct.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that AT&T's Q1 2026 EPS will be $0.54, just below the consensus of $0.55. While the Street correctly recognizes AT&T's stable core operations, I believe consensus is underestimating two headwinds: (1) intensifying telecom competition that will pressure service revenue growth and margins more than expected, and (2) continued negative volatility in non-operating income that consensus models as more predictable. Historical analysis shows non-operating items swinging wildly (-$6.23B to +$4.53B over last four quarters), yet consensus appears to assume a normalized level. My projection of $6.15B operating income reflects stability but acknowledges competitive headwinds highlighted in recent news, while my -$440M non-operating income projection incorporates historical volatility rather than assuming reversion to a benign mean.

Key data points driving my variant view include: AT&T's operating income range of $5.75-$6.55B over the last four quarters suggests limited upside beyond the midpoint; recent news of intensifying telecom competition in 2026 (Bernstein note) directly contradicts bullish narratives about pricing stability; and the company's Q4 2025 EPS beat of +10.6% was driven by non-operating items rather than operational improvements, creating an unsustainable base. The stock's recent pre-market slip ahead of CFO commentary suggests market nervousness about subscriber trends and cash flow visibility.

I would change my mind if: (1) management provides concrete evidence of successful pricing discipline in the face of competitive pressures, (2) non-operating items show meaningful stabilization in the quarter, or (3) fiber growth accelerates beyond historical patterns to offset wireless pressures. Without these catalysts, I expect AT&T to meet but not exceed lowered expectations.

forecasts.thesis:
Consensus is mismodeling the efficiency of AT&T's cost transformation and the structural benefit of the Q1 revenue mix. While Q1 is seasonally the weakest for revenue due to lower equipment volumes, this mix shift is distinctively margin-accretive because equipment is sold at near-zero or negative gross margins. The street is extrapolating top-line seasonality directly to the bottom line without accounting for this composition change.

Furthermore, my analysis of the $2B+ cost savings program indicates structural OpEx reductions are now hitting the P&L in force, specifically in SG&A, which should decline as a percentage of service revenue. The market remains skeptical of T's execution history, but the last 3 quarters show a clear trend of beating on profitability even when revenue is in-line. I project a $0.02 EPS beat driven by Gross Margin expansion to ~60.5% (vs ~59.5% modeled by consensus implieds) and disciplined SG&A.

Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that if promotional intensity spikes—triggered potentially by Verizon's need to regain share—my margin assumptions would be at risk. A resurgence in handset subsidies would directly erode the profitability thesis. However, current channel checks suggest a rational competitive environment favoring profitability over volume chasing.

Excluding those non-cash items, Tilray's normalized quarterly loss has been in the $0.00 to -$0.05 range, which I believe is the appropriate baseline. The key differentiator in my forecast is the granular SG&A analysis - I'm projecting $94M vs what appears to be Street estimates closer to $100M+, as I believe the Q2 spike included truly one-time items that won't recur.

What would change my view: (1) If management commentary suggests SG&A will remain elevated above $100M for operational reasons, I would revise EPS down to -$0.08; (2) If cannabis pricing shows signs of stabilization or recovery, I could see upside to both revenue and margins; (3) Any early revenue recognition from Carlsberg pre-2027 would be a positive surprise not in my forecast. The Carlsberg deal remains the key 2027+ catalyst, but provides no Q3 benefit.

My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.01 remains 50% below Wall Street's $0.02 consensus, driven by continued fundamental disagreement about Tanzania's mining tax regime. Now six days post the Feb 19 roadshow with CEO/CFO, there has been ZERO public disclosure of tax guidance or clarity on the effective rate going forward. The empirical evidence from Q1 2026 is unambiguous: the company reported a 111% effective tax rate ($7.0M tax expense on $6.3M pre-tax income), resulting in a net loss despite strong operational performance. Wall Street's $0.02 consensus implicitly assumes an effective tax rate of 30-35%, which I believe is demonstrably unrealistic based on actual results.

The operational story at Buckreef remains compelling: revenue has tripled YoY, gross margins are holding at 56%, and production is ramping toward 18,500 oz quarterly targets. At $2,050/oz gold prices, this supports $38M quarterly revenue and ~$19M operating income - genuinely impressive execution. However, the path from operating income to EPS is where the Street and I diverge. My 65% effective tax rate assumption for Q2 (vs Q1's 111%) already incorporates significant normalization, yet still results in materially lower EPS than consensus. Tanzania's mining royalties (6% on gold revenue), corporate taxes, withholding taxes, and deferred tax timing create structural tax burdens that Q1 data suggests Wall Street is underappreciating.

What would change my view: (1) Public disclosure from management quantifying expected effective tax rates going forward, (2) Evidence that Q1's 111% rate included one-time items that won't recur, or (3) Tanzanian regulatory changes reducing mining taxation. Until such evidence emerges, I'm maintaining my below-consensus stance with low conviction given the binary nature of the tax question.

Similarly, if the Cintas $275 offer is withdrawn or materially modified, the operational distraction could intensify. The EVP insider sale on February 17, while executed under a pre-arranged plan, warrants monitoring for additional selling activity that could signal management concerns about deal completion or operational headwinds.

Quantitatively, I’m modeling a Q2 gross margin near ~35.0% (down sequentially vs Q1 but above the depressed level implied by a much lower EPS on flat revenue) and holding SG&A roughly flat-to-slightly up sequentially. That produces operating income of ~$29.6M and net income of ~$22.8M, which with ~18.1M diluted shares yields $1.26.

I would change my view if (1) operating expenses print materially above ~$186M (e.g., outsized professional fees) or (2) cost of revenue rises enough to push gross margin meaningfully below ~34.5% on essentially flat revenue—either would pull EPS below consensus quickly given limited top-line volatility.

However, none of these warning signs are present in current data. I maintain high conviction that Unity will beat the $1.37 consensus by a meaningful margin, with my $1.58 estimate representing a conservative outcome given the historical beat pattern.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.52 remains 7% below consensus of $1.63, reflecting a more cautious view on seasonal refining margin compression that I believe the Street is underweighting. While I've revised upward slightly from $1.48 based on better-than-expected mid-February crack spread data ($14-15/bbl vs initial $12-14 estimate) and the positive development of Venezuelan crude imports providing feedstock cost advantages, Q1 remains historically Valero's weakest quarter. The disastrous Q1 2025 (-$1.90 EPS) was driven by major turnaround activity and margin compression, but even normalizing for that, the seasonal pattern shows Q1 gross margins typically compress 40-50% from Q4 peaks.

The Street appears to be extrapolating Q4 2025's strong $3.82 EPS beat too aggressively into Q1. While throughput should be higher year-over-year (2.85M bpd vs 2.7M bpd) due to absence of major turnarounds, crack spreads remain 25-30% below Q4 levels. The renewable diesel segment continues to be a ~$150-180M quarterly drag with no near-term RIN relief in sight, despite the positive JetBlue SAF partnership announcement. I'm also flagging the Benicia regulatory scrutiny and Ardmore wrongful death lawsuit as potential sources of unexpected charges, though probability of Q1 impact is low.

What would change my view: If March crack spreads strengthen materially above $16/bbl, I would revise upward toward consensus. Conversely, if China demand data disappoints or if the Venezuelan crude import arrangement faces political disruption, downside to $1.30-1.40 is possible. forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2025 forecast of -$0.14 EPS on $135M revenue remains unchanged from my prior estimate as the information vacuum persists with now a 5+ week earnings delay without ANY company communication. This unprecedented delay for a public company—extending well past the typical 60-day post-quarter reporting window without an 8-K explanation, press release, or investor update—is itself the most material signal available. Well-functioning public companies simply do not miss their reporting obligations by this margin without providing explanations unless facing material audit complications requiring extensive work, potential restatements, or going concern qualification discussions that prevent timely filing.

The underlying business fundamentals, while severely challenged, would likely show modest sequential improvement from the Q2 2025 disaster (-$1.51 EPS) if reported normally. The Obagi Lip Therapy launch in early February 2026 and Milk Makeup's continued positioning in prestige beauty suggest revenue around $135M is achievable. However, the balance sheet remains existentially challenged with projected ending cash of approximately $5M—barely enough for 1-2 weeks of operations. The company urgently requires a capital raise that will likely come at highly dilutive terms given the securities investigation overhang and operational distress.

The key insight the market may be missing is that the extended delay itself likely signals problems beyond typical reporting issues. The 30% stock decline mentioned in January news reflects some concern, but the complete communication blackout for over a month suggests the situation may be worse than current valuations imply. My low confidence level (0.25) reflects the impossibility of accurate forecasting in an information vacuum—the actual results could range from a modest loss if operations stabilized to a massive charge if impairments, restatements, or going concern issues emerge.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 FY26 EPS estimate of $1.36 remains $0.03 (2.2%) below Street consensus of $1.39, reflecting continued skepticism about the pace of SG&A normalization. The central thesis is unchanged: Q1 FY26 SG&A spiked to $63.5M—well above the historical $51-54M run rate—driven by distribution network transition costs that management explicitly stated won't yield benefits until FY27. While I expect modest sequential improvement to ~$62M in Q2 as some one-time transition costs abate, this remains structurally elevated. The Street appears to be pricing in faster cost normalization than the evidence supports.

The revenue build supports $161M for Q2, representing healthy 4.3% sequential growth driven by Americas seasonal strength and stable EMEA performance. This aligns with historical Q1-to-Q2 patterns where maintenance product demand peaks. Gross margin faces modest pressure at 55.3% (vs Q1's 56.2%) as elevated inventory from Q1's $84M build flows through COGS—a mechanical effect the Street may be underweighting. The key variance driver remains operating leverage: with SG&A at $62M on $161M revenue, operating income reaches ~$27M, generating net income of ~$19.9M and EPS of $1.36 on 13.55M diluted shares.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that distribution transition costs are wrapping up faster than FY27, (2) A significant surprise in gross margin performance suggesting inventory cost flow-through is more favorable, or (3) Material revenue upside beyond $163M that provides operating leverage despite elevated SG&A. The Ken Plunk board appointment is operationally neutral—adding CFO expertise but with no immediate earnings catalyst. Insider buying patterns remain encouraging but don't affect near-term estimates.

forecasts.thesis:
I’m modestly above the Street on EPS ($1.60 vs $1.56) because the setup from Q4 2025’s elevated SG&A ($12.12B vs ~$9–10B in prior quarters) still argues for meaningful (though not complete) expense normalization in Q1 2026. My differentiated view is that the Street is likely underweighting the probability that Q4 contained transitory cost items, but over-weighting the speed of NII re-acceleration given sticky funding costs.

On revenue, I model a seasonal step-down to ~$30.7B from $31.82B in Q4 2025, with net interest income easing to ~$12.10B (from $12.33B). I add only a mild tailwind to market-sensitive fees rather than a big swing, using peer commentary as directional support but not a primary driver.

I would change my view if (1) evidence emerges that Q4’s cost base is structural (compliance/operational) and persists into Q1, or (2) early credit indicators force a more meaningful provision build than my baseline; either would pull EPS toward or below consensus even if revenues hold up.

forecasts.thesis:
I am maintaining my ¥43.50 Q4 2026 EPS estimate, representing a 6.2% discount to the Street consensus of ¥46.39. My variant view centers on continued skepticism about the pace of margin recovery: while Q4 should see meaningful seasonal improvement from Q3's severely depressed 7.3% operating margin, I project only 10.7% recovery versus the 11.0%+ embedded in consensus. The key constraint remains the persistent inventory overhang at ¥216.5B, which improved only modestly in Q3 despite management's destocking efforts. Until inventory normalizes closer to ¥200B, YASKAWA's pricing power and margin efficiency will remain constrained.

The fundamental demand picture remains stable but unexciting. MKS's Q4 2025 earnings call confirmed semiconductor equipment stabilization, which provides modest support to the Robotics segment, but this is insufficient to offset broader headwinds. China exposure (~30% of revenues) continues to be a drag, and peer results from Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries confirm that automation demand is stable but not accelerating. Q4 seasonal patterns should help - historically YASKAWA's strongest quarter - but I do not see the catalysts for a meaningful beat versus my conservative estimate.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of accelerating China demand or successful market share gains, (2) Inventory reduction to ¥205B or below indicating normalized supply chain, (3) Management guidance raise or pre-announcement of stronger-than-expected results. Conversely, risks to my estimate include worse-than-expected China weakness or yen volatility. My confidence level remains medium given the cyclical uncertainty and limited visibility into demand trends.

My $39.50 EPS forecast reflects gross margin compression to 34.3% (vs 36.4% in Q4 2025) and interest expense of ~$485M (vs $527M in Q4 2025 but still elevated). The last-year Q4 EPS level (44) anchors my view that Q4 can print strong, but I do not underwrite a meaningful step-up above that without direct evidence.

I would change my mind (toward consensus or above) if there is concrete evidence of accelerating Robotics orders/backlog and/or explicit margin guidance implying higher utilization and richer mix; conversely, I’d cut EPS if FX or one-time charges emerge or if Robotics demand softens into quarter-end.
